exampleContent.text:
Most companies that say they care about code quality don't actually measure it.

They have a style guide. They do code reviews. They talk about tech debt in planning meetings.

But they don't have a number.

Three years into Meridian I realized we'd been managing code quality by vibes. Felt bad, improve it. Felt good, ship it. No baseline, no trend, no accountability.

The thing is — you can't improve what you don't measure. And you can't measure it if you haven't decided what 'it' is.

We spent two weeks defining our quality metrics. Not the standard ones. Ours — specific to how we build and what we care about.

Now we review them monthly. The conversations are different. Specific instead of vague. Actionable instead of philosophical.

If you're not measuring code quality with a number, you're not managing it.

Something I got wrong for the first two years: I thought better tools would make my team more productive.

We bought Notion. Then Linear. Then we tried five CI/CD pipelines. I kept looking for the tool that would unlock us.

Here's what I've learned — tools don't make teams productive. Clarity does.

The engineers who ship the most aren't using the best tools. They're working on things with a clear definition of done, a clear owner, and a clear timeline.

When we finally got that right, we stopped switching tools. The ones we had were fine.

A boring observation, maybe. But it saved us eighteen months of tool-switching and onboarding overhead.
